lessons.title: Hooke's law, stress, strain and the Young modulus
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — properties of matter (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State Hooke's law, use F = kx and calculate the energy stored in a stretched spring or wire
Define stress, strain and the Young modulus and use them for a wire
Interpret force–extension and stress–strain graphs (limit of proportionality, elastic limit, plastic deformation)
reviewNotes: Young modulus of steel is quoted as about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa; the data sheet of the board may give a different rounded value.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Hooke's law
blocks.md:
Within the **limit of proportionality** the extension x of a spring or wire is directly proportional to the force F: **F = kx**, where k (N m⁻¹) is the **force constant** (stiffness).

Springs in **series**: 1/k = 1/k₁ + 1/k₂ (softer). Springs in **parallel**: k = k₁ + k₂ (stiffer).

The energy stored (elastic potential energy) is the area under the F–x graph: **E = ½Fx = ½kx²**.

blocks.title: Stress, strain and Young modulus
blocks.md:
**Stress** σ = F/A (Pa = N m⁻²). **Strain** ε = extension/original length = x/L (no unit). In the proportional region the ratio is constant:

**Young modulus E = σ/ε = FL/(Ax)** (Pa). It depends on the material, not on the size of the sample.

Typical value for steel: about 2 × 10¹¹ Pa (a textbook value; check your table).

blocks.caption: Force–extension graph: linear up to the limit of proportionality, then curving.
blocks.alt: A graph of force against extension, a straight line to a red point marked limit of proportionality and a curve flattening beyond it.

blocks.title: Behaviour beyond Hooke's law
blocks.md: Beyond the **elastic limit** the material is permanently stretched (**plastic deformation**) and does not return to its original length when the load is removed. At the **yield point** the extension increases with little extra force, and the material finally breaks at the breaking stress. A **brittle** material (glass) breaks with little plastic deformation; a **ductile** one (copper) stretches a lot.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using the total length of the wire after stretching as L: use the **original** length.
- Converting diameter instead of radius: A = π(d/2)², with d in metres (0.80 mm = 0.80 × 10⁻³ m).
- Mixing up the limit of proportionality (Hooke's law fails) with the elastic limit (permanent deformation starts); they are close together but not identical.
- Forgetting the ½ in the energy stored.

blocks.title: Example 1 — A spring
blocks.statement: A spring has force constant k = 200 N/m and is stretched by 0.15 m. Find the force applied and the energy stored.

blocks.title: Example 2 — A steel wire
blocks.statement: A steel wire of length 2.0 m and diameter 0.80 mm carries a load of 100 N. Take E = 2.0 × 10¹¹ Pa. Find the stress, the strain and the extension.

lessons.title: Density, pressure and fluids
lessons.programRef: GCE Advanced Level Physics — properties of matter (to be checked against the official syllabus)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Define density and pressure and use p = ρgh for the pressure due to a liquid column
Use Archimedes' principle to find upthrust and explain floating
Apply the equation of continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) and the idea of terminal velocity in a viscous fluid
reviewNotes: Bernoulli's equation may not be on the syllabus at this level; it is only mentioned.
Atmospheric pressure is taken as 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa (1.01 × 10⁵ Pa in more precise tables).
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Density and pressure
blocks.md:
**Density** ρ = m/V (kg m⁻³); fresh water 1000 kg m⁻³. **Pressure** p = F/A (pascal, Pa = N m⁻²).

In a liquid at rest the pressure at depth h is **p = ρgh** (plus the atmospheric pressure at the surface, about 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa). It depends on depth and density, not on the shape of the container, and acts equally in all directions.

blocks.title: Upthrust and floating
blocks.md:
**Archimedes' principle**: the upthrust on a body fully or partly immersed in a fluid equals the weight of the fluid displaced: **U = ρ_fluid V_displaced g**.

A body **floats** when upthrust = weight. For a floating body: ρ_body/ρ_fluid = fraction of its volume submerged. A body sinks if its average density exceeds the fluid's.

items.text: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ : narrower pipe, faster flow

blocks.caption: Equation of continuity: the fluid speeds up in the narrow section.
blocks.alt: A pipe narrowing from a wide section on the left to a narrow section on the right, with arrows showing faster flow in the narrow part.

blocks.title: Fluids in motion
blocks.md:
For an incompressible fluid in a pipe, the **equation of continuity** says the volume flow rate is constant: **A₁v₁ = A₂v₂** (narrower section, faster flow).

For smooth (streamline) flow of a non-viscous liquid, Bernoulli's equation relates pressure and speed: p + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant (included for completeness; check the syllabus). In a **viscous** fluid a falling sphere reaches a terminal velocity when weight = upthrust + viscous drag.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Forgetting atmospheric pressure when the question asks for the **total (absolute)** pressure; the gauge pressure is ρgh alone.
- Using the volume of the whole body for upthrust when only part is submerged.
- Confusing density and relative density (relative density has no unit).
- Converting cm³ to m³ wrongly (1 cm³ = 10⁻⁶ m³).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Pressure in water
blocks.statement: Find the extra pressure and the total pressure 10 m below the surface of a lake (ρ = 1000 kg m⁻³, g = 9.8, atmospheric pressure 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa).

blocks.title: Example 2 — A submerged block
blocks.statement: A steel block of mass 15.6 kg and volume 2.0 × 10⁻³ m³ is lowered fully into water. Find the upthrust and its apparent weight in water.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style (g = 9.8 m/s²)
exercises.prompt: A spring (k = 80 N/m) is stretched by 0.25 m. Find the force (N).

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style (g = 9.8 m/s²)
exercises.prompt: A 150 N force acts on a wire of cross-section 3.0 × 10⁻⁶ m². Find the stress (10⁷ Pa).
exercises.explanation: σ = F/A = 150/3.0 × 10⁻⁶ = 5.0 × 10⁷ Pa, i.e. 5.0 in units of 10⁷ Pa.

exercises.prompt: True or false: the Young modulus of a material depends on the length of the wire used.
exercises.explanation: E is a property of the material; length and area cancel out in FL/Ax.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style (g = 9.8 m/s²)
exercises.prompt: Two identical springs, each k = 200 N/m, are joined in series. What is the force constant of the combination (N/m)?
exercises.explanation: 1/k = 1/200 + 1/200 = 1/100, so k = 100 N/m. (In parallel it would be 400 N/m.)

exercises.explanation: x = FL/AE: L ×2 and A ×4 gives x × 2/4 = ½ the original extension.

exercises.prompt: Water flows at 2.0 m/s in a pipe of diameter 4.0 cm into a section of diameter 2.0 cm. What is the speed in the narrow section (m/s)?
exercises.explanation: A ∝ d², so A₂ = A₁/4 and v₂ = 4 × 2.0 = 8.0 m/s.

exercises.source: Original exercise, GCE Advanced Level style (g = 9.8 m/s²)
exercises.prompt: A cube of wood (density 600 kg m⁻³) floats in water. What fraction of its volume is submerged (give a decimal)?
exercises.explanation: Fraction = ρ_wood/ρ_water = 600/1000 = 0.60.
